## 1. Purpose

This procedure describes the grinding and homogenization of dried soil,
sediment, plant tissue, and other solid environmental samples to
produce a fine, uniform powder suitable for chemical, elemental, and
isotopic analysis. Many analytical methods require a homogeneous
subsample of 0.5--20 mg (e.g., EA-IRMS capsules,
[SOP-L414](SOP-L414-soil-ea-irms.qmd)) or 0.5--1.0 g (e.g., acid
digestion, [SOP-L410](SOP-L410-hotplate-acid-digestion.qmd),
[SOP-L411](SOP-L411-mars-microwave-digestion.qmd)). Without thorough
grinding and homogenization, small subsamples may not represent the
bulk sample, introducing analytical error unrelated to the method
itself.


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Dry grinding and homogenization of air-dried or
  oven-dried (60--105 C) solid samples, including mineral soils,
  organic soils, sediments, dried plant tissue, compost, and biochar,
  using agate or steel mortar and pestle, ball mill, or mechanical
  grinder
- **Does not apply to:** Wet grinding or homogenization of fresh
  tissue (cryogenic grinding for molecular biology applications);
  sieving-only sample preparation (see
  [SOP-F400](../field_sops/SOP-F400-soil-sampling.qmd) for 2 mm
  sieving); bead beating for DNA extraction (integral to
  [SOP-L700](SOP-L700-dna-extraction.qmd))
- **Location:** EA Program laboratory, SGM 134


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                              |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI            | Approve SOP                                 |
| Lab Manager       | Maintain grinding equipment, replace worn components |
| Trained Personnel | Grind and homogenize samples per this SOP   |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use    |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Dust inhalation:** Grinding dry soil and plant tissue generates
  fine respirable dust. Perform grinding inside a fume hood or wear
  a dust mask (N95 or equivalent). Soils from contaminated sites
  (lead, arsenic, pesticides) pose additional inhalation hazards.
- **Noise:** Ball mills and mechanical grinders can be loud; wear
  hearing protection during extended grinding sessions.
- **Silica dust:** Grinding mineral soils releases respirable
  crystalline silica, which is a chronic inhalation hazard. Always
  use the fume hood for mineral soil grinding.
- **Pinch/crush hazards:** Ball mill jars and mechanical grinder
  components are heavy. Handle with care; secure jars before starting
  the mill.
- **Cross-contamination:** Residual sample in grinding equipment can
  contaminate the next sample. Thorough cleaning between samples is
  essential (see Section 6.5).
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Safety glasses
- [ ] Lab coat
- [ ] Nitrile gloves
- [ ] N95 dust mask (or work in fume hood)
- [ ] Hearing protection (ball mill or mechanical grinder)

### Emergency Procedures

For dust inhalation, move to fresh air. For cuts from broken
equipment, apply first aid. Refer to
[SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd).

### Grinding Equipment

| Item                                  | Location  | Best For                         |
|:--------------------------------------|:----------|:---------------------------------|
| Agate mortar and pestle (various sizes) | SGM 134 | Small batches (less than 50 g); trace metal work (low contamination) |
| Ceramic (porcelain) mortar and pestle | SGM 134   | General purpose; not for trace metals (may contribute Al, Si) |
| Ball mill (planetary or mixer mill)   | SGM 134 (if available) | Large batches; consistent particle size; high throughput |
| Mechanical grinder (e.g., Wiley mill, Thomas mill) | *TBD* | Plant tissue; coarse initial grinding |

### Accessories

| Item                                  | Notes                          |
|:--------------------------------------|:-------------------------------|
| Stainless steel spatula               | For transferring sample        |
| Brush (soft bristle, nylon)           | For cleaning mortar and mill jars |
| Lint-free wipes (Kimtech)             | For wiping surfaces            |
| 70% ethanol spray bottle              | For decontamination            |
| Compressed air (can or line)          | For blowing dust from crevices |
| Test sieves (No. 60 = 250 um; No. 100 = 150 um; No. 200 = 75 um) | For verifying particle size if required |
| Labeled sample vials or coin envelopes | For storing ground samples    |
| Analytical balance                    | Per [SOP-L200](SOP-L200-analytical-balance-calibration.qmd) |


## 6. Procedure

### 6.1 Sample Selection and Drying

1. Samples must be thoroughly dried before grinding. Use air-dried
   samples sieved to 2 mm (per
   [SOP-F400](../field_sops/SOP-F400-soil-sampling.qmd)) or oven-dried
   samples per the analytical SOP:
   - 60 C for plant tissue and soils intended for nitrogen or carbon
     isotope analysis (higher temperatures alter delta-15-N;
     [SOP-L414](SOP-L414-soil-ea-irms.qmd))
   - 105 C for soils intended for total carbon, LOI, or metals (where
     isotope fractionation is not a concern)
2. Record the drying temperature and duration in the lab notebook

### 6.2 Mortar and Pestle (Manual Grinding)

1. Place a clean, dry mortar on a stable bench surface. If working
   with contaminated soil or generating visible dust, place the mortar
   inside a fume hood.
2. Add a small amount of dried sample (5--20 g) to the mortar
3. Grind with a circular and pressing motion, periodically scraping
   material from the sides of the mortar back to the center
4. Continue grinding until the sample passes through the target sieve
   (typically No. 60 [250 um] for general chemistry or No. 100
   [150 um] for EA-IRMS). For plant tissue, grind until a uniform fine
   powder is achieved.
5. Transfer the ground sample to a labeled vial or coin envelope using
   a clean spatula
6. Record the sample ID and particle size achieved

::: {.callout-tip}
For very hard or fibite samples (e.g., woody roots, calcium
carbonate nodules), pre-crush coarsely with a hammer inside a thick
plastic bag before transferring to the mortar. This reduces grinding
time and wear on the mortar.
:::

### 6.3 Ball Mill (Mechanical Grinding)

1. Select the appropriate grinding jar and ball material:
   - Agate: for trace metal work (minimal contamination)
   - Stainless steel: for general chemistry (faster, but may
     contribute Fe, Cr, Ni)
   - Zirconia: good compromise (hard, low contamination)
2. Load the sample into the jar (fill no more than one-third of the
   jar volume to allow ball movement)
3. Add grinding balls per the manufacturer's recommendation (typically
   1:10 ball-to-sample mass ratio for a planetary mill)
4. Secure the jar in the mill and close the lid
5. Set the speed and duration per the analytical SOP or the following
   general guidelines:

   | Sample Type      | Speed (rpm) | Duration  | Target Size |
   |:-----------------|:------------|:----------|:------------|
   | Mineral soil     | 300--400    | 5--10 min | less than 150 um |
   | Organic soil     | 200--300    | 3--5 min  | less than 250 um |
   | Dried plant tissue | 200--300  | 2--5 min  | fine powder  |
   | Sediment         | 300--400    | 5--10 min | less than 150 um |

6. Run the mill. If the mill heats the sample (some models do),
   alternate grinding intervals with 1-minute rest periods.
7. Open the jar carefully (dust may escape). Transfer the ground
   sample to a labeled container.
8. If required, verify particle size by passing a subsample through
   the target sieve.

### 6.4 Mechanical Grinder (Plant Tissue)

1. For dried plant tissue (leaves, stems, roots), a Wiley-type or
   Thomas-type cutting mill provides rapid coarse grinding
2. Set the screen mesh to the target particle size (typically 1 mm
   [No. 18] or 0.5 mm [No. 35])
3. Feed dried tissue into the hopper slowly; do not overload
4. Collect the ground material from the output chamber
5. For analyses requiring finer particle size (e.g., EA-IRMS), follow
   with mortar and pestle or ball mill to reduce further

### 6.5 Cleaning Between Samples

Cross-contamination is the primary quality risk in grinding. Clean
thoroughly between every sample:

1. Disassemble the mortar/pestle or mill jar and balls
2. Brush out all visible residue with a soft-bristle brush
3. Wipe all surfaces with a lint-free tissue dampened with 70% ethanol
4. For trace metal work: rinse with 10% HNO~3~, then triple-rinse
   with DI water, and dry
5. For isotope work: rinse with DI water, wipe with ethanol, and blow
   dry with compressed air. Residual organic matter from the previous
   sample can bias delta-13-C and delta-15-N values.
6. For the Wiley mill: run a small amount of clean quartz sand through
   the mill between samples to abrade residual material from the
   cutting chamber, then brush and wipe
7. Allow all equipment to dry completely before grinding the next
   sample

::: {.callout-important}
If grinding a series of samples with very different compositions (e.g.,
alternating between high-carbon compost and low-carbon mineral soil),
grind a "sacrificial" subsample of the next sample and discard it to
purge residual contamination from the previous sample. This is
especially important for EA-IRMS work.
:::

### 6.6 Storage

1. Store ground samples in labeled vials, microcentrifuge tubes, or
   coin envelopes
2. Store at room temperature in a desiccator or sealed container
   (ground samples are hygroscopic due to increased surface area)
3. For long-term storage, seal tightly and store in a cool, dry
   location
4. Record the grinding date, equipment used, and particle size in the
   lab notebook and on the sample label


## 7. Quality Control

- Verify particle size for at least 10% of samples by passing a
  subsample through the target sieve. All material should pass; if
  not, re-grind.
- For trace metal work: periodically grind a certified reference
  material (CRM) and analyze alongside samples to check for
  contamination introduced by the grinding equipment
- For isotope work: grind and analyze a known reference material
  (e.g., USGS-40, USGS-41) periodically to verify that grinding does
  not introduce isotopic bias
- Document the grinding equipment and material (agate, steel, zirconia)
  used for each batch, as different materials can introduce different
  trace elements


## 8. Waste Disposal

| Waste Type                    | Disposal Method                          |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Grinding residue (non-hazardous soil/plant) | Standard trash or return to sample stock |
| Grinding residue (contaminated soil) | Chemical waste per [SOP-L006](SOP-L006-waste-disposal.qmd) |
| Quartz sand (cleaning aid)    | Standard trash                           |
| Used ethanol wipes            | Standard trash                           |
| Worn grinding balls or jars   | Standard trash (agate, ceramic) or metal recycling (steel) |

## 11. Training Record

Before grinding samples independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Demonstrate proper use of the mortar and pestle, including
   grinding technique and cleaning between samples
3. If using the ball mill: demonstrate proper jar loading, speed/time
   selection, and jar cleaning under supervision
4. Grind at least 5 samples under supervision with acceptable particle
   size verification (all material passes the target sieve)
5. Be signed off by the PI or lab manager
